examples: Every time I watch this movie, I can't help being moved.
When I see cake, I can't help eating it, even though I'm on a diet.
Seeing how hard he worked, I couldn't help crying.
That punchline is so funny that I can't help laughing.
When I think something is unfair, I can't help saying so.
When he heard the news, he too couldn't help crying out with joy.
fields.explain:
Often used with the adverbs つい／思わず to emphasize spontaneity.
Has an emotional nuance; used a lot in narratives and personal comments.
Not suitable for expressing obligation/rules; in that case use ～ざるを得ない／～ねばならない.
Used in the past tense when talking about a reaction that has already happened: ～ずにはいられなかった.

• Expresses an inner urge/emotion that the speaker cannot hold back, so they end up doing V: "cannot help but…/feel compelled to (out of emotion)".
• Often used with verbs expressing natural reactions: 笑う、泣く、言う、拍手する、謝る、触る、見直す…
• Unlike ～ざるを得ない (forced by external circumstances), this pattern is driven by inner feelings.
• The subject is usually the speaker; if it is someone else, there must be grounds/observation for the conjecture.
fields.notes:
• Formally a double negative, but the meaning is a strong affirmative: "cannot not V" = "will surely V".
• When the subject is someone else, add evidence: ～ようだ／～に違いない to sound less presumptuous.
• Everyday spoken language often uses the variant ～ないではいられない because it is easier to pronounce.
meaning_vi: Cannot help but…, cannot hold back/suppress…
examples: 1. ①　〈映画について〉
A: 泣いてるの？
B: だって、あのラストシーンを見たら、泣かずにはいらないよ。
2. ②　A:　何一人で笑ってるの？
B:　あの時の先生の顔を思い出すと、笑わずにはいられなくて。
explain: Used when emotions/impulses drive an action; it is natural, not intentional.
Formal written language uses ～ずにはいられない; natural spoken language uses ～ないではいられない.
Combines with emphatic adverbs: どうしても/つい/思わず/あまりに… + ～。
Avoid overusing it for actions that require reason/strong will (signing contracts, surgery…).
examples: 1. その話を聞いて、泣かないではいられなかった。
When I heard that story, I couldn't hold back my tears.
2. どうしても気になって、見ないではいられなかった。
I was so curious that I couldn't help looking.

common_mistakes: • Confusing it with ～てしまう in questions that ask you to distinguish the nuances "could not hold back" vs "ended up".
• Using it for a third-person subject without adding ようだ/らしい → an unfounded conjecture.
• Wrong conjugation of する: ×しずにはいられない → correct: せずにはいられない。

fields.connection: V plain form + だけあって だけのことはあって / N / Na + な / Aい
examples: As you'd expect from a shop that always has a line, everything you order there is delicious.
Being young, he wasn't afraid of anything and took on all kinds of challenges.
As you'd expect from the home of beer, Germany has many kinds.
As you'd expect from a famous shop, it is always full of customers.
As befits a song that became a hit all over the world, both the singer and the melody are wonderful.
True to being called an insect expert, that child really does know a lot about bugs.
fields.explain:
Used to acknowledge a reasonable cause-and-effect relationship with a nuance of "praise that is well deserved".
Often used together with さすが to emphasize the acknowledgment: さすが～だけあって...
Style: natural in both spoken and written language; suits polite contexts.
The second clause is a result that meets expectations; rarely used with commands/intentions.

• States a cause ("worthy of/truly") that leads to a reasonable result, usually praising or acknowledging value.
• Evaluation nuance: mostly positive; sometimes neutral, rarely direct criticism.
• Often used in comments on quality, ability, brands, depth of experience, status.
• Order: [Reason (characteristic)] + だけあって、[a well-deserved result].
fields.notes:
• When a noun comes before another noun: NのN + だけあって: 彼の出した論文の質は、研究者だけあって高い。
• It can still be used with a mildly negative evaluation if the result is "only natural": 都会だけあって、騒音がひどい。
• Not used for desires: 高いだけあって、買いたい× → Use a comment, not an intention.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～だけに: test questions often ask you to distinguish the nuances "well-deserved praise" vs "precisely because... all the more...".
Wrong particle attached to a na-adjective: 有名だだけあって× → 有名なだけあって✓.
A command/intention in the second clause is unnatural: 高いだけあって、買いましょう×.

rows: <ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いだけあって、<ruby>美味<rt>おい</rt></ruby>しい。
Emphasizes degree; can also be used with negative/contrasting results
<ruby>期待<rt>きたい</rt></ruby>しただけに、がっかりだ。
Usually placed at the end of the sentence as a comment
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>しただけのことはある。
Exclamatory adverb; can be used with だけあって

fields.meaning:
～だからやはり（当然(とうぜん)）、～だからなおさら
Because
fields.connection: V plain form + だけに / N / Na + な / Aい
examples: Having worked there for 20 years, Mr. Tanaka knows a lot about the company.
He lived in America as a child, so naturally his English is good.
Having been in Japan for as long as 10 years, he knows a lot about Japanese affairs.
Because this model is the most popular one right now, I hear it's hard to get hold of.
Because it was such a tough match, I'm all the happier that we won the championship.
Precisely because everyone's expectations are so high, failure is not allowed.
fields.explain: ◎ Has the form 「AだけにB」, expressing that from fact A, the assertion or result B naturally follows. Used in spoken language more than 「～だけあって」.
fields.notes: Means that, contrary to the good result that would normally be expected, the opposite happened. Used when a bad result, contrary to what was expected, came about.

fields.meaning: As expected…, no wonder… (worthy of the reputation/effort put in)
fields.connection: V plain form + だけ(のことは)ある / N / Na + な / Aい
examples: Aoki, your English is good. That's what studying abroad in Canada does for you.

A: These Italian shoes are 100,000 yen, apparently.
B: Wow. But they're worth the price. The shape and color are really nice.
fields.notes: Means that something is worthy of the effort, status or experience. Expresses a positive evaluation of the corresponding results, ability, features, etc. (193)

fields.meaning: At least…, it could be worse…
fields.connection: V plain form + だけましだ / N + である / Na + な / Aい
examples: The pay is low, but at least I have a job.
I got caught in the rain, but at least there was no thunder.
There were mistakes, but at least it didn't turn into a major accident.
It's an old apartment, but at least it's close to the station.
We lost the game, but at least we weren't shut out.
I was late, but at least I was able to attend the class.
fields.explain:
Has a nuance of consoling oneself/seeing the minimum positive side; strongly subjective.
Often used in conversation and everyday comments; not very formal.
The first clause can state the bad side; the clause with ～だけましだ states the saving grace.

• Relative evaluation: it falls short of the desired standard, but is still better than a worse situation.
• Often implies consolation, self-consolation, or seeing the minimum positive side.
• Can be accompanied by an explicit comparison with ～だけましだ＋ほう／他と比べて..., but it is usually implicit.
fields.notes:
• The negative form is rare: ～だけましではない（not even "at least"） is seldom used; restructuring the sentence is preferred.
• Often combined with まあ/さすがに/せめて to strengthen the nuance: せめて無事だっただけましだ。
• In colloquial speech: だけマシ, だけでもマシ have a casual nuance.
mistakes: Using it for absolute praise is incorrect: "最高だ" × → ～だけましだ is relative praise, not absolute.
Wrong attachment to N/Na: Nであるだけましだ／Naなだけましだ. Avoid using Nだ/Naだ before だけましだ in written language.
Confusing it with まだまし／～ほうがましだ: exam questions often ask you to choose between a pattern of direct comparison vs one evaluating the current situation.

rows: At least..., it could be worse...

examples: It's impossible. Someone like me could never do it.
The other team won the championship last time. There's no way we can win, I'm telling you.
Memorizing 100 kanji by the end of today is impossible. There's no way I can do it.
I don't think anyone would ever believe a story like this.
"There's no way you could ever understand how I feel, Mom!"
Starting now, there's no way we'll make it in time.
fields.explain:
Casual, decisive tone; can sound a bit "blunt" or impolite depending on the context.
Better suited to expressing personal judgments than objective, proven facts.
Common with the verbs: 間に合う、できる、起きる/起きられる、覚える、わかる、勝つ、治る.
When you need to be polite/in writing: switch to ～はずがない・～わけがない・～可能性は低い.

• Strong negative assertion: "no way, cannot possibly, absolutely not".
• Shows the speaker's subjective conviction (confident conjecture, strong emotion).
• Used in conversation; sometimes sounds rather blunt.
• Often used with potential verbs, result verbs, and verbs expressing possibility/time.
fields.notes:
• "っこ" is a colloquial suffix that adds emphasis, also seen in other forms such as "やりっこない (rare)".
• Often appears in drama/manga dialogue to show a straightforward attitude.
• In many cases the potential form is more natural: 覚えられっこない, 起きられっこない.
mistakes: Using it in formal writing: × っこありません → Use instead: ～はずがありません/～わけがありません.
Attaching to the wrong verb stem: × 覚えるっこない → correct: 覚えられっこない (use the potential).
Confusing the nuance with ～ないだけ: っこない is absolute negation, not "simply not".
JLPT multiple-choice questions often test recognition of "colloquial, strong negation" and the structure Vます＋っこない.

fields.meaning: Looks like, seems; tending toward ~, full of ~ (e.g. 水っぽい)
examples: She's a high school student, but she always wears grown-up-looking clothes.
The room didn't seem to get cleaned very often, and it was dusty.
My younger brother gets bored easily, so he's always wanting something new.
Maybe it's my age, but I've become forgetful lately. People's names, little errands, and so on.
a dusty room
whitish clothes
fields.explain:
"N + っぽい" expresses an outward appearance/general air, without asserting the actual nature.
"Vます + っぽい" turns a tendency into an adjective: 飽きっぽい（easily bored）, 怒りっぽい（quick-tempered）.
When describing people, it easily takes on a critical nuance: 子どもっぽい（childish）. Be careful in formal communication.
Expresses color/substance: 黒っぽい（blackish）, 茶色っぽい（brownish）, 油っぽい（oily/greasy）.

• Meaning 1: "similar to/like N" in appearance or general impression. Example: 子どもっぽい（childish, immature）.
• Meaning 2: "tends to V easily" (forgetful, easily bored…). Usually has a somewhat negative nuance.
• Meaning 3: "has the color/quality of N" (blackish, greasy, watery…).
• Nuance: casual, colloquial; used for impressionistic, subjective descriptions; can carry mild criticism when describing people.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～みたい／～よう.
→ ～っぽい has a colloquial nuance, "seems/full of/similar to", and sometimes indicates a tendency.
2) Often carries a subjective feeling or evaluation.
→ Not formal; usually used in conversation.
3) Be careful, as it can mean "easily/often".
→ Cases like 忘れっぽい (forgetful) are tendencies and a trap for mechanical translation. meaning_vi: Overflowing, full of, steeped in ⏐ explain: Usually used in spoken language. Used to describe things, situations, or people that are imbued with a certain quality. ⏐ examples: 1. あの小学生は、大人っぽい。
That elementary school student is so grown-up.
2. この料理は油っぽくていやだ。
This dish is very oily, so I don't like it meaning_vi: Like…, similar to…, seems like… ⏐ explain: Expresses the feeling "it feels like", it seems like… ⏐ examples: 1. 年を取ると、忘れっぽくなる。
As you get older, you become forgetful.
2. このコート、デザインはいいけれど、生地が安っぽいね。
This coat has a nice design, but the fabric looks cheap, doesn't it?
mistakes: Using っぽい about people in formal language can be crude/impolite: ×社長は子どもっぽい → better to avoid.
Confusing it with らしい: 男っぽい（somewhat masculine-looking, may not be the real thing） ≠ 男らしい（truly manly）.
Attaching it at random to Vます is rare: ×走りっぽい（unnatural）. Only a few familiar verbs such as 忘れる/飽きる/怒る…
Misunderstanding the strength: っぽい is subjective, a feeling; it does not assert an objective fact.

rows: Attaches to emotions/character (<ruby>得意<rt>とくい</rt></ruby>げ/<ruby>寂<rt>さび</rt></ruby>しげ)
Mild, more objective than っぽい

examples: As this report shows, the earth's population is approaching its limit.
The company's performance is gradually improving.
The population is increasing in urban areas.
Demand for online education is growing.
Endangered species are decreasing year by year.
Ways of working are becoming more diverse.
fields.explain:
Objective nuance, describes trends; rarely used in casual conversation.
Good with time-series data/charts: 増加しつつある傾向、低下しつつある割合.
Not used with commands, volition, or invitations.
Often accompanied by adverbs and time expressions: ますます、徐々に、次第に、年々、徐々に～しつつある.

• Expresses a trend/change that is ongoing and likely to continue in the present.
• States a transitional state, "in the process of" rather than "having reached".
• Often appears in academic language, newspapers, and reports: objective, formal.
• Often used with verbs of change: 増える、減る、広がる、進む、深まる、弱まる、安定する(しつつある).
fields.notes:
• Often used with nominalization: ～しつつある＋N (例: 変化しつつある社会, 失われつつある文化).
• Combined with evaluation: ～しつつある一方で、～／～しつつあるが、～ (stating a contrast).
• In newspaper headlines: 「～が広がりつつある」 is concise, neutral, and easy to read.
mistakes: Wrong structure: × V辞書形＋つつある → correct: Vます(without ます)＋つつある.
Using it with punctual verbs: × 到着しつつある (if you mean "on the way", use instead: 到着に向けて進んでいる).
Confusing it with Vている: つつある emphasizes a trend of change, not just a state that is happening.
The JLPT often asks you to recognize the formal style and the combination with verbs of change.
